front.title: Extending Normalized Forms to String-Derived Types

abstract.t: YANG models frequently define identifiers using string or string-derived types whose lexical space permits multiple representations of the same underlying value. This can lead to incorrect behavior when semantically equivalent values are compared lexically.
This document add an optional extension to the existing YANG concept of normalized form to string-derived types whose lexical space permits multiple representations of the same underlying value.

section.name: Introduction
section.t:
YANG
treats values of type string as lexically distinct; equality and uniqueness are therefore determined by exact string comparison.
YANG defines normalized representations for many built-in data types. Canonical or normalized forms provide a unique representation of a value independent of how it may have been entered or encoded.

For string-derived types, YANG currently provides no mechanism to define a normalized form distinct from the lexical representation. As a result, semantically equivalent values that have multiple valid lexical representations may not compare equal and may not be detected as duplicates.

This issue has been observed in both IETF and IEEE YANG modules, leading to interoperability problems and incorrect duplicate detection. Existing YANG typedefs such as mac-address (, ) define syntax but do not define normalized comparison semantics.

A prominent example is the representation of MAC addresses in YANG. IETF and IEEE modules define different lexical forms for MAC addresses, and equivalent values may not compare equal when represented using different valid formats. This problem is described in
.

While MAC addresses provide a clear motivating example, the underlying issue is more general. YANG lacks a mechanism for schema authors to define normalized forms for string-derived types whose lexical space permits multiple representations of the same underlying value.
The resulting normalized form is used for equality and uniqueness operations. The original lexical representation is preserved for encoding and retrieval.

This mechanism is intentionally non-invasive. Existing YANG modules remain valid and unchanged. The extension is applied only where normalized forms are needed and has no effect on implementations that do not support it.

section.name: Problem Statement
section.t: When string-derived types permit multiple lexical representations of the same value, the following issues can arise:

ul.li: Semantically equivalent values may not compare equal.
Duplicate entries may not be detected in keyed lists.
Leaf-list uniqueness constraints may be violated.
XPath equality comparisons may yield incorrect results.

section.t: Pattern restrictions alone do not solve this problem, because they validate syntax but do not affect comparison semantics.

section.name: Design Goals
section.t: The solution defined in this document:

ul.li: MUST preserve the lexical representation of values.
MUST apply to equality and uniqueness operations.
MUST be minimally invasive to existing YANG modules.
MUST be opt-in and backward compatible.
MUST be general across string-derived types.

section.name: Overview
section.t: This document defines a YANG extension that allows a string-derived type to specify a normalization algorithm.
The resulting normalized form is used for equality comparisons, list key uniqueness, and leaf-list uniqueness. The original lexical representation is preserved for encoding and retrieval.

This extension does not modify the YANG language and does not require changes to existing typedef definitions. The extension may be attached to existing types, derived types, or schema nodes where normalized form behavior is desired. Implementations that do not understand the extension continue to process the lexical type normally. Implementations that advertise support for the extension apply the specified normalization algorithm for equality and uniqueness operations.
Use of this extension does not, by itself, change the behavior of implementations that do not support it.

section.name: YANG Extension Definition
Semantics
section.t: If a type includes the normalized-form extension:

ol.li: A normalized form MUST be derived using the specified identity.
Equality comparisons, including = and != , MUST use the normalized form.
List key uniqueness MUST be enforced using the normalized form.
Leaf-list uniqueness MUST be enforced using the normalized form.
The lexical representation MUST NOT be modified solely to satisfy this extension.

section.name: Normalized identity
section.t: Normalized forms are identified by identity and are associated with a deterministic algorithm.

section.name: mac-48
section.t: The mac-48 identity applies to 48-bit MAC addresses represented as six hexadecimal octets. The lexical representation is defined by the type that uses the extension.
The normalization procedure is:

ol.li: Validate the input against the lexical pattern.
Use the resulting 12 hexadecimal digits as the normalized form of the MAC address.

section.name: List Key Example
section.t: A list key using the IETF typedef continues to accept only the IETF colon-separated lexical form. A corresponding IEEE model can use the IEEE typedef and preserve the IEEE dash-separated lexical form. In both cases, the shared mac-48 normalized form enables consistent equality and duplicate detection across representations.

section.name: Backward Compatibility
section.t: Existing YANG models are unaffected unless the extension is used. Lexical representation is preserved. Behavior changes only affect comparison and uniqueness.

section.name: Applicability
section.t: While motivated by MAC addresses, this mechanism can apply to any string-derived type with multiple equivalent representations, including case-insensitive identifiers, formatted identifiers, and normalized encodings.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Normalization reduces ambiguity and helps prevent duplicate or conflicting configuration entries.
Implementations MUST ensure that normalization algorithms are deterministic and unambiguous.
